claims.statement: In the Udumbarikasihanada Sutta (DN 25), about 30% of the text consists of passages repeated verbatim two, three or four times, another 35% involves repetition with minor modifications at a primary level, and in total almost 87% involves quantifiable repetition of one kind or another (restating Allon 1997).
claims.scope: One discourse, hand analysis of the Pali prose; 'primary level' repetition; 13% does not recur within the sutta (much of it recurs in other suttas).

quantities.name: dn25_share_words_in_within_sutta_repeated_8grams
quantities.unit: share of words covered by an 8-word sequence occurring >= 2 times in the same sutta (Pali root text)

quantities.name: dn25_rank_among_dn_mn_by_repetition
quantities.unit: share of the 186 DN+MN suttas with LOWER 8-gram coverage than DN 25 (90/186 lower, 96 higher)
quantities.baseline: corpus median 0.546 (IQR 0.413-0.652) vs DN 25 0.539; corr(log length, coverage) = 0.15

our_assessment.why: The structure holds up, and DN 25 is a fair choice: by within-sutta repeated n-grams it sits at the median of all 186 Digha and Majjhima suttas, so 'a typical sutta is mostly repetition' is supported -- 54% of a median sutta's words lie in 8-word sequences it repeats. The absolute numbers depend on what counts as repetition. Verbatim n-gram coverage of DN 25 (45-54% for 8-12-word repeats) is HIGHER than Allon's 30% verbatim figure, probably because coverage counts first occurrences too, or because his 'passages' are larger primary units. His verbatim + minor-modification total (65%) matches 4-gram coverage (0.649) closely. His 87% is not reached by any contiguous n-gram measure (0.695 at n=3), because it includes structural repetition with several substitutions. So '87% of Buddhist suttas are repetitions', as the figure is often re-quoted, mixes one sutta with all suttas (here harmless: the sutta is typical) and a structural definition with a verbatim one (not harmless: the number belongs to the definition).
